lesson.title: The Electron Thief: Identifying the Oxidizing Agent
lesson.summary: An oxidizing agent is the species that causes another substance to be oxidized by accepting its electrons, which means the oxidizing agent itself is reduced.
lesson.body:
This is the single most commonly flipped idea in the whole redox unit, so read this definition slowly and precisely: the oxidizing agent is the species that gets reduced. It does the oxidizing to something else by taking that something else's electrons for itself, which means the oxidizing agent's own oxidation number goes down, not up. Students often guess the opposite, assuming the oxidizing agent must be the one that gets oxidized, because the two words look related. They are related, but as opposites: the oxidizing agent causes oxidation in another species precisely by undergoing reduction itself.

Look back at the permanganate and iron reaction from the last chapter. Manganese in MnO4- dropped from oxidation number +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons, so MnO4- was reduced. Because MnO4- is the species that got reduced while causing Fe2+ to be oxidized to Fe3+, MnO4- is the oxidizing agent in this reaction. It is the electron acceptor, not the electron donor.

Common oxidizing agents share a family resemblance: they tend to contain an atom in an unusually high oxidation state, hungry for electrons to bring that number down, or they tend to be highly electronegative elements that attract electrons strongly on their own. Familiar examples include O2, the halogens such as Cl2, hydrogen peroxide H2O2, dichromate ion Cr2O7 2-, and concentrated nitric acid. In every case, these species are reduced as they do their oxidizing.

Here is a fast way to identify the oxidizing agent in any redox reaction without extra work: scan the reactant side, find the species whose central atom's oxidation number goes down over the course of the reaction, and that species is your oxidizing agent. Always look on the reactant side. It is a common mistake to name a product, like Mn2+, as the oxidizing agent, but the agent is whatever species you started the reaction with, before it was reduced.
